title: 15-year-old claims AI helped crack 300-year-old math puzzle
key_facts: Jung Gi-hyo, a ninth grader at Gimpohangaram Middle School in Gyeonggi, posted a paper titled 'The rhombicosidodecahedron is not Rupert' on Zenodo and GitHub on 5 Oct 2026.
He claims to have disproved, with AI help, that this solid (20 triangles, 30 squares, 12 pentagons) can pass through a hole in an identical copy of itself, a counterexample to the Rupert property.
He used Claude to generate code and then reviewed the results; the calculations took about 38 hours on his laptop.
His Reddit post topped a Claude coding forum on Saturday; reactions were sharply divided.
Jung says he cannot independently verify every detail but another paper reached the same conclusion around the same time by a different approach.
Oum Sang-il (Institute for Basic Science): posting on a repository records the date but does not guarantee validity.
Seo In-suk (professor of mathematical sciences, Seoul National University): an author must understand every aspect of the work.
quote_evidence: "I am not at a level where I can independently verify every detail of the paper," Jung said.

"Posting a paper on a research repository establishes a public record of when it was released, but it does not guarantee the validity of its contents," said Oum Sang-il, chief investigator of the Discrete Mathematics Group at the Institute for Basic Science.
why_it_matters_hint: A teenager's AI-assisted claim shows the new reach of AI for amateurs and the unsettled question of how such work is checked.
event_date: Paper posted 5 Oct 2026; JoongAng report 13-14 Oct 2026
notes: Older news re-dated: the paper was posted on 5 Oct 2026; the JoongAng report is dated 14 Oct 2026. Claim is unreviewed.
